proposals.name: Load-bearing reformulation that itself yields the method
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract recasts the problem into a different formal language, and how directly that recast generates the proposed algorithm. 10: an explicit change of representation is stated (e.g. 'we interpret graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures', 'we frame OOD detection as statistical hypothesis testing', 'we treat the graph as a hyperparameter and use meta-gradients', 'we cast defense as a minimax zero-sum game, whose optimal play is a mixed strategy') AND the method is presented as a consequence of that recast: delete the reformulation and the method could not have been derived. 5: a fresh framing is announced but the method would stand without it (framing is decoration). 0: no reformulation at all; the contribution is an architecture, loss term, or module inserted into an existing pipeline and described entirely in that pipeline's own vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: The strongest reformulate-then-derive items are exactly where the scorecard sits far below the dense reading: R02 (integral transform -> Monte Carlo -> batched training), R07 (heuristic -> hypothesis test with p-values), R08 (bilevel attack -> graph-as-hyperparameter), R53 (defense -> mixed strategy), R58 (quantization -> l-infinity perturbation -> l1 gradient penalty). A criterion bank built around 'is there a method, is it evaluated' cannot see this move at all. The mirror cases are R48 and R59, where a familiar mechanism is dropped into a new slot with no change of formalism.

proposals.name: Subtractive contribution: equal or better with a requirement removed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the central claim is that something previously required is no longer needed, while quality is retained. Count removals of: an auxiliary loss or supervision signal, access to data or model internals, a training or fine-tuning stage, a trained component, or an assumption about the deployment setting. 10: the headline is a removal, stated plainly, with a retention-of-quality claim attached (e.g. adversarial supervision alone makes the perceptual loss superfluous; the final classifier layer can be fixed with little or no loss; training no longer needs test data present; the attack assumes no knowledge of or access to the target classifier; the detector needs no retraining and no prior knowledge of the test distribution). 5: mixed, one thing removed and another added. 0: the method strictly adds requirements (extra module, extra stage, extra supervision, extra tuned hyperparameters) and nothing is removed.
proposals.rationale: Doing more with strictly less is a classic expert quality signal and is invisible to a bank that credits presence of components. R09, R35, R02, R08 and R07 are all removals and all sit well above their scorecard rank; R11 (adds a smoothness constraint plus distillation to make reconstruction work) and R06 (adds AIRL plus a binary-action DQN switch) are pure additions and sit above their dense rank.

proposals.name: Mechanism parsimony versus a stack of mutually propping patches
proposals.instruction: Score whether one mechanism does the work. 10: a single idea carries the result; anything else mentioned is bookkeeping. 5: two components, each independently motivated. 0: an enumerated stack of three or more parts where later parts exist mainly to repair problems created by earlier parts, signalled by chains such as 'first we define three mechanisms ... then to reduce variance we perturb ... finally', or 'PAPO consists of i) an encoding to avoid training collapse, ii) a hypernetwork, iii) the size as an extra input', plus a separate training procedure to make the whole thing trainable. Judge the architecture of the contribution, not its length.
proposals.rationale: Patch-stacks read as technical depth to a criterion bank (more components to score as 'technically substantial') but read as fragility to an expert. R46, R17, R06 and R11 are all stacks and all sit far above their dense rank, while the parsimonious R30 (one modified diffusion kernel), R35 and R53 sit far above their scorecard rank.

proposals.name: Design choices forced by a stated analysis
proposals.instruction: Score whether each nontrivial design decision is preceded by an argument that makes that choice the one to make: a proof, a derivation, a spectral or complexity analysis, or an explicitly diagnosed failure mode. 10: the reader can reconstruct why this choice and not a neighbouring one, e.g. a proved identity (KL between stochastic processes equals the supremum of marginal KLs) that the training objective is then built on; a loss expansion whose first-order term is what gets regularized; a complexity analysis of the only strictly equivariant layer that motivates the two new layers. 5: motivation by analogy to a success elsewhere ('motivated by the success of Transformers', 'inspired by heap allocation'). 0: choices are simply announced ('we propose', 'we adopt', 'we also employ') with no reason given.
proposals.rationale: R34, R58 and R38 all show the derivation chain and all rank far higher under the dense reading than the scorecard's; R20, R50 and R40 announce their components with only analogy as motivation and rank far higher under the scorecard's. Argument-to-design traceability is judgeable from the abstract but is not the same thing as 'has theory', which is why a bank with a theory checkbox misses it.

proposals.name: Formal claims quantified, with the conditions they hold under
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of any theoretical statement. 10: rates, sizes or complexities are given explicitly along with the setting they hold in, so a reader could in principle contradict them (coreset of size O(m + poly(k/eps)) constructible in near-linear time; at most O~(d^2 H^5 / eps^2) trajectories within H deployments under a linear MDP with feature dimension d; complexity reduced from O(C^2 L^5) to O(C L^3 log L) while remaining strictly equivariant). 5: a named theorem or property with partial conditions. 0: theory vocabulary with no content the reader can restate: 'we give theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative', 'produces lower-variance gradient estimates', with no assumptions, no rate, no comparison point. Score 0 also when there is no formal claim.
proposals.rationale: Precise-theory abstracts are the most extreme dense-high / card-low cases in the slice (R45, R57, R38, R24): they carry no benchmark table, no ablation and often no code, so a criterion bank organized around empirical hygiene has nothing to credit, while the quantified statement is the whole contribution. R60 and R31 assert properties in the same register without quantification, and are the mirror direction.

proposals.name: Improvement stated against prior results rather than prior systems
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract identifies the specific prior claim it displaces. 10: names prior results (with authors, venue, bound, or exact prior guarantee) and states exactly how this work improves on them, including whether the improvement is near-optimal or matched by a lower bound (improving on a bound with exponential dependence on m+k and on a weaker bi-criteria guarantee; being the first to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal dimension dependence simultaneously; naming the exact previous complexity being reduced). 5: prior methods named generically ('previous OOD detection heuristics', 'attention-based NAS') with a qualitative comparison. 0: positioning consists only of 'state-of-the-art' or a benchmark ranking, with no identification of which prior claim is now false or superseded.
proposals.rationale: R45 and R57 anchor themselves to specific prior theorems and are near the bottom of the scorecard while mid-to-high for the dense model; R38 does the same with complexities. By contrast R50 and R32 position purely against leaderboards and sit far above their dense rank. Naming the displaced claim is a real quality signal that leaderboard-shaped criteria cannot express.

proposals.name: Guarantee grade of the headline claim
proposals.instruction: Score the epistemic strength of what is actually promised. 10: certification, exactness, or error control -- a certificate of robustness for all remaining samples and the exact adversarial accuracy determined for the first time; a p-value per test sample with Type I error provably maintained under composition of detectors; proved local convergence and avoidance of strict saddles in all differentiable games; strict (not approximate) equivariance preserved. 6: a proven property under restrictive assumptions, or a guarantee about the estimator rather than the task. 3: consistent estimation or unbiasedness claimed without rate. 0: only an average-case empirical improvement is offered.
proposals.rationale: R24 and R07 both trade heuristic average-case claims for guarantees, and both are rated much higher by the dense model than the scorecard; R43 does the same on the theory side. A bank scoring 'are results strong' treats a guarantee and a benchmark win as the same kind of evidence, which is precisely the collapse this criterion undoes.

proposals.name: Critique of a shared practice, with a corrected protocol supplied
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract identifies something the whole subfield does and shows it to be wrong, ill-defined, or unfairly measured, and then supplies the corrected version. 10: a named shared practice is overturned and a replacement is given, e.g. stored models not being counted against the memory budget rendering comparisons unfair, plus a demand to evaluate across aligned memory scales; a widely used term shown to lack coherent meaning in standard statistical frameworks, plus a causal reframing and a resource; a universally trained component shown to be near-worthless. 5: a limitation of a single named competitor is identified and fixed. 0: the standard setup is accepted without examination.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R26 both attack the measurement conventions of their subfields rather than a competitor, and both are read much higher by the dense model; R35 belongs to the same family. A criterion bank scores the method a paper proposes, so a paper whose main product is a corrected way of measuring is systematically under-credited.

proposals.name: Core construct distant from recombination of standard components
proposals.instruction: Score how far the central object is from something producible by pairing two known ingredients. 10: a construct a well-read reader would not have generated by recombination -- higher-dimensional attention updating entities with tensor products of value vectors; adversarial defense implemented as a randomized mixed strategy over activations; a curvature invariant from optimal transport generalized to hypergraphs with proved properties. 5: a known idea carried into a genuinely different regime where it is not obvious it should work. 0: the contribution is fully described by 'known mechanism A applied to setting B' -- attention but across layers, self-paced learning but in hyperbolic space, ensembles but for hyperparameter ranking, a hypernetwork but conditioned on population size.
proposals.rationale: R33 and R53 are terse, number-free abstracts that a criterion bank has almost nothing to score, yet the idea in each is strange in the way real novelty is strange; R08 is a third case. The dense model places these very high while the scorecard does not. R48, R50, R32 and R46 are all cleanly describable as A-applied-to-B and are the over-credited direction.

proposals.name: Results sentence falsifiable rather than adjectival
proposals.instruction: Score whether the empirical claim names what was compared, on what, and in which direction, so that a reader could go and dispute it. 10: fully checkable, e.g. training orders of magnitude more efficient with predictions comparably accurate against a named model family; small perturbations pushing graph networks below a baseline that ignores all relational information, and transferring to unsupervised embeddings. 5: comparison named but direction only qualitative. 0: 'extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method' with no named comparison; or superiority asserted with no evaluation described anywhere in the abstract. Do not reward numeric density as such -- reward whether the claim is checkable.
proposals.rationale: R04, R27 and R42 close with unfalsifiable effectiveness sentences, and R31 and R47 assert advantages ('massive decreases in computation time', 'significantly improved clustering performance') with no evaluation identified at all -- yet each is rated well above its dense rank, suggesting the bank credits the presence of a results sentence rather than its content. R02 and R08 show the checkable form.

proposals.name: Restraint in self-description of one's own results
proposals.instruction: Score the register in which the authors describe their own findings. 10: flat reporting that includes where the method merely ties or where the gain is small ('predictions remain comparably accurate', 'with little or no loss of accuracy', 'comparable or better results'). 5: neutral but uniformly favourable. 0: self-praise and surprise markers carry the claim -- 'Surprisingly, it can boost the performances by a large margin', 'the significant superiority of PAPO over baselines', 'brings remarkable performance gain', 'we demonstrate the superiority of our amalgamated optimizer'. Judge tone about the paper's own results only; enthusiasm about the problem area is not penalized.
proposals.rationale: Promotional register clusters hard in the direction the scorecard over-credits (R48, R46, R20, R32, R17), while the understated R02 and R35 are both read much higher by the dense model. A judge asked 'are the results strong' reads confident phrasing as strength; an expert reads unhedged superlatives as a warning and reads a volunteered tie as a credibility signal.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth organized by a question, not tallied
proposals.instruction: Score whether the scale of evaluation exists to answer a stated question, and whether the answer is reported as a finding about the phenomenon rather than as a win. 10: the sweep is the instrument for a question and the answer is stated with structure -- e.g. asking where and how much language-specific capacity matters and answering that 10-30 percent placed at top and/or bottom layers is best and that one-to-many benefits more than many-to-one; or asking whether random permutations are optimal and answering differently per function class, from exponential gap to none. 5: broad evaluation plus one incidental observation. 0: breadth reported as a tally -- a count of baselines, search spaces, datasets or tasks followed by a single aggregate superiority statement.
proposals.rationale: R32 (12 baselines, 16 search spaces, 86 tasks), R29 (6 long-text and 8 short-text corpora) and R40 (a list of five datasets) all convert breadth into a single aggregate claim and all sit far above their dense rank -- a bank with an 'evaluation thoroughness' criterion scores the count. R13 and R56 use comparable breadth to produce structured findings instead.

proposals.name: Reusable artifact of substance, beyond a repository link
proposals.instruction: Score what the paper leaves behind that others can use independently of its headline system: a dataset, a benchmark or evaluation protocol, a general framework subsuming other methods, or a technique explicitly flagged as of independent interest. 10: such an artifact is described concretely and its reuse value is legible (public release of both original and counterfactually revised datasets; an exploration-preserving policy discretization and generalized G-optimal design offered as independently useful; a framework that unifies existing black-box attacks and accepts arbitrary priors). 5: a general method claimed to be architecture-agnostic but demonstrated in one pipeline. 0: the only shareable output is code that reproduces this paper's own numbers. Judge substance; the presence or absence of a URL must not move the score.
proposals.rationale: Code links cluster strikingly on the over-credited side (R48, R49, R50, R16, R17, R25 all carry URLs and sit above their dense rank) while R08, R33 and R53 carry none and sit far below their dense rank -- a bank crediting artifact availability is likely rewarding the URL. R26 and R57 show what substantive reusability looks like without that signal dominating.

proposals.name: Problem exists outside the paper that solves it
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract establishes that someone other than the authors already has this problem. 10: the obstacle is stated in pre-existing terms -- a model that cannot be trained without test data present and whose neighbourhood expansion is infeasible on large dense graphs; the need to certify networks before deployment; distributional failures that are costly in production lines, autonomous vehicles and healthcare. 5: a plausible but generic motivation ('X is an important problem in Y'). 0: the problem is coined by the paper itself, so that its importance rests on the paper's own framing and its success is measured against ingredients the paper chose -- 'we study a new problem named Optimizer Amalgamation', judged against the very optimizers it amalgamates -- or the promised applications are never named.
proposals.rationale: R17 defines its own problem and grades itself against its own components; R11 ends on 'two applications ... demonstrating the capabilities' without naming a use; both are read far higher by the scorecard than the dense model. R02, R24 and R07 anchor to obstacles that predate them and run the other way. A bank scoring 'is the motivation clearly stated' cannot distinguish a real external need from a well-written self-declared one.

proposals.name: Finding survives parity: informative even without a margin
proposals.instruction: Imagine the reported performance numbers were replaced by 'comparable to existing methods'. Score how much of the contribution survives. 10: essentially all of it -- the claim teaches something about the object of study that stands on its own (a heavily parameterized standard component contributes marginally; once memory is accounted for consistently, saving models does not consistently help; the choice of loss function shapes double descent through the Hessian spectrum at the interpolation threshold). 5: partly -- a mechanism or diagnosis remains, but the case for it rests on the margin. 0: nothing survives; the delta over baselines is the entire content.
proposals.rationale: R35, R14 and R01 remain worth reading with the numbers deleted and are read much higher by the dense model than by the scorecard, which has little to score in an abstract whose product is a fact rather than a system. R49, R59 and R20 are wholly constituted by their reported improvements and run the other way; this criterion is the direct antidote to a bank that credits margin size.

proposals.name: Asymptotic-bound and theorem-proving register density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much of this abstract's language is formal-theory apparatus: big-O or tilde-O complexity expressions, epsilon/delta accuracy parameters, dimension and horizon symbols, named duality or convergence results, 'we prove', 'we derive a bound', 'lower bound', 'strictly equivariant complexity', and inline mathematical notation. 0 = none of this register anywhere; 5 = a theorem or bound is mentioned once among mostly plain prose; 10 = the abstract is dominated by it, stating several distinct formal objects, bounds or proofs. You are measuring how much of this vocabulary is PRESENT, as a proportion of the text. Do NOT judge whether the theory is correct, deep, novel, hard or valuable, and do not treat theory papers as better or worse than empirical ones.
proposals.rationale: Rows written in the complexity-bound register sit at the extreme floor of the scorecard while the dense model finds them unremarkable-to-ordinary: R16 (card_pct=0.004; tilde-O(d^2 H^5 / eps^2) trajectory bound, G-optimal design, information-theoretic lower bounds), R01 (card_pct=0.013; eps-coreset of size O(m + poly(k eps^-1))), R58 (card_pct=0.038; local convergence and strict-saddle proofs), R56 (card_pct=0.056; influence-function bounds on population loss), R37 (card_pct=0.124; O(CL^4) and O(CL^3 log L) layers). A bank of natural-language criteria has almost nothing to tick on such text -- no dataset roll-call, no percentage gains, no application story -- so the REGISTER, not the merit, is doing the moving. Register is a topic/style marker, not research quality.

proposals.name: Quantified improvement claims stated with units
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract states numeric performance figures with explicit units or metric names: percentage accuracy deltas, FID, mIoU, box/mask AP, ROUGE, MAE, nats per image, parameter counts, FLOPs, speed multipliers, 'orders of magnitude'. 0 = no such number anywhere; 5 = one or two figures on a single metric; 10 = many figures spread over several metrics, tasks or datasets. Count occurrences and prominence only. Do NOT assess whether the numbers are large, whether the gains are meaningful, whether the comparison is fair, or whether the measurement was done well.
proposals.rationale: Number-dense abstracts are exactly the scorecard's favourites in this slice: R11 (card_pct=0.983 vs dense_pct=0.568; '1.6% Top-1', '0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs', '3-4% box AP and mask AP'), R44 (card_pct=0.885 vs dense_pct=0.094; '10.9% and 12.4% improvement in MAE'), R12 (card_pct=0.774 vs dense_pct=0.158; 'beats the SVM by 6.12%, achieving 96.32%'), R25 (card_pct=0.701; '41.58 nats/image', '66.24 nats/image'). The mirror image is R08 (card_pct=0.359 while dense_pct=0.996) and R58 (card_pct=0.038), which state no figures at all. Whether results are compressed into the abstract as numbers is a writing convention that varies by subfield and era; tagged mixed because having a clean headline number to quote is partly downstream of actually having a result.
proposals.upstream_parent: the sub-community's benchmark-table reporting convention and the authors' habit of foregrounding headline figures in the abstract

proposals.name: Abstract length and count of distinct declarative claims
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 on sheer extent of text and elaboration: approximate word count together with the number of separate declarative claims, sub-contributions or enumerated points the abstract makes. 0 = under roughly 80 words, two or three sentences, one claim; 5 = a conventional single-paragraph abstract of roughly 150-200 words with three or four claims; 10 = 300 words or more with many enumerated sub-claims, itemised contributions and multiple result statements. Measure size and claim-count only. Brevity is NOT a fault and length is NOT a virtue -- do not judge how well written, thorough or padded the abstract is.
proposals.rationale: The shortest items in the slice are all dense-high / card-low: R08 (three sentences, card_pct=0.359 against dense_pct=0.996), R17 (about 90 words, card_pct=0.222 against dense_pct=0.699), R59 (card_pct=0.449 against dense_pct=0.722). The longest, most enumerated items are card-high: R60 ('Our contributions are three-fold. First... Next... Finally...', card_pct=0.709), R30 (card_pct=0.799), R09 (card_pct=0.654). A fixed bank of criteria can only fire on text that exists, so a longer abstract mechanically offers more surface for criteria to match, independent of what the paper did. This is a pure text-volume proxy.

proposals.name: Code and artifact release announcement
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract announces released artifacts: a repository URL, 'code is available at', 'we release our code and models', pretrained checkpoints, a call to build on the release. 0 = no mention of any artifact; 3 = a bare promise such as 'we will release the data'; 7 = an explicit live URL; 10 = URL plus models or checkpoints plus an explicit invitation to reuse. Score presence and prominence of the announcement only. Do NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, whether the artifact sounds useful, or whether the release makes the work more credible.
proposals.rationale: Six of the highest scorecard percentiles in the slice all carry a release clause while the dense model is unmoved: R11 (github URL, card_pct=0.983 vs dense_pct=0.568), R34 ('we release our code and models', card_pct=0.949 vs dense_pct=0.573), R44 (card_pct=0.885 vs dense_pct=0.094), R39 (github URL, card_pct=0.816 vs dense_pct=0.449), R52 (github URL, card_pct=0.645 vs dense_pct=0.218), R50 (code and pre-trained models URL, card_pct=0.765 vs dense_pct=0.214). Conversely the dense-high / card-low rows R08, R17, R20 and R38 carry no release clause. The clause is one sentence of boilerplate produced by a lab's engineering practice and by what year it is; it is not a property of the finding. Mixed because a lab with the staff to ship a clean repo often also has the staff to run better experiments.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing lab's engineering resources and open-source norms, plus the platform-era convention that artifact links belong in the abstract

proposals.name: Evaluation inventory: named datasets, baselines, explicit counts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 by how many distinct named resources the abstract enumerates -- benchmarks, datasets, tasks, architectures, competing methods -- and whether it states explicit counts of them ('five datasets', '12 baselines', '16 search spaces', '86 datasets/tasks', 'three established datasets'). 0 = no named resource at all; 5 = two or three named datasets or baselines; 10 = a long roll-call spanning several modalities, tasks or dozens of enumerated items. Count named items and stated counts only. Do NOT judge whether the evaluation is appropriate, sufficient, well-chosen or convincing, and do not treat a bigger roll-call as better science.
proposals.rationale: Roll-call breadth tracks the scorecard and not the dense model: R35 (card_pct=0.697 vs dense_pct=0.385; '12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks'), R03 (card_pct=0.692 vs dense_pct=0.402; 'CIFAR, SVHN, STL-10, ImageNet and Cityscapes'), R30 (card_pct=0.799; ImageNet, TIMIT, speech, translation), R48 (card_pct=0.662; CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet). Compute-poor but pointed entries such as R08 and R58 read as empty to the same bank. How many benchmarks appear is largely set by how many GPUs and how many co-authors were available, an upstream resource fact whose only textual fingerprint is the roll-call itself. Mixed because resources also buy genuinely more thorough work.
proposals.upstream_parent: the compute budget, GPU access and engineering headcount behind the submission

proposals.name: Period stamp of the topic and benchmark vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the vocabulary, model names, baselines and benchmarks date the text to an identifiable period of the field, and say which period. Earlier-period markers: RNN encoder-decoder, ROUGE on CNN/DailyMail, MNIST or CIFAR-10 as the main testbed, 'the GCN recently proposed by Kipf and Welling', graph kernels and graph2vec, MuJoCo meta-RL, straight-through quantisation, imperceptible-perturbation adversarial framing. Later-period markers: large Transformers as world models, pretrained-LM and zero-shot framing, hyperbolic or spectral self-supervision, conference-year strings embedded in repository URLs. 0 = vocabulary is period-neutral and could have been written in any year; 10 = the text is unmistakably stamped to one period. Score the strength of the period stamp only. Do NOT judge whether work from that period is better or worse, more or less novel, or more or less relevant.
proposals.rationale: The dense-model extreme of this slice is almost entirely early-period text: R20 (dense_pct=0.991; stochastic activation pruning, minimax defence framing), R57 (dense_pct=0.987; MIP verification of MNIST classifiers), R29 (dense_pct=0.974; RNN encoder-decoder summarisation scored by ROUGE on CNN/DailyMail), R38 (dense_pct=0.925; meta-gradient attacks on GCNs), R02 (dense_pct=0.904; 'the GCN recently proposed by Kipf and Welling'). Whichever edition an abstract belongs to is fixed before anyone reads it, and its only trace in the text is dated vocabulary. A model that has read the period's literature can recognise period-typical text without that recognition tracking merit. Mixed because a period's most-reproduced work is often genuinely strong.
proposals.upstream_parent: which conference edition / calendar year the submission belongs to (position of the container itself in the run of editions), and the resulting chance the exact text was absorbed during model pretraining

proposals.name: Insider shorthand and assumed-known predecessor systems
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract writes for an in-group reader: specialist acronyms used unexpanded or expanded once then reused heavily (TM, LM, LS, SDP, AOL, E2E, PDM, DGN, GCL, HPO), predecessor systems named as though already familiar to the reader ('the Kanerva Machine', 'DocNADE', 'fBNNs', 'convex potential layers', 'Almost-Orthogonal-Layer'), and notation or symbols introduced without gloss. 0 = fully self-contained for a general machine-learning reader; 5 = a couple of subfield terms assumed; 10 = essentially unreadable without subfield membership. Score the amount of assumed shared context only. Do NOT judge whether the abstract is clear, well written, or whether concision is appropriate here.
proposals.rationale: In-group-addressed abstracts cluster on the scorecard-high side: R09 (card_pct=0.654 vs dense_pct=0.333; stacks TM, LM, LSTM-LM, DocNADE, ctx-DocNADE, ctx-DocNADEe in a single paragraph), R25 (card_pct=0.701 vs dense_pct=0.252; extends 'the Kanerva Machine' as an assumed-known object), R52 (card_pct=0.645 vs dense_pct=0.218; AOL, SDP, SLL, convex potential layers as given), R41 (card_pct=0.415 vs dense_pct=0.128; assumes BNNs and fBNNs are already understood). Dense scoring of raw text is comparatively unimpressed. Assumed shared context is a fact about who the authors talk to at workshops, not about what they found; a criterion bank rewards the dense terminological scaffolding it produces. Mixed because deep subfield embedding also produces genuinely well-aimed contributions.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' embeddedness in one narrow subcommunity and the in-group audience they are writing toward

proposals.name: Unedited-English surface irregularity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of surface irregularities in the English: article and agreement slips ('The most GCNs suffer the performance loss'), non-idiomatic verb complements ('we task humans with revise each document'), strained collocations ('exhibiting potentials to stride towards'), inconsistent capitalisation inside a title, spacing or hyphenation slips, literal-translation phrasing. 0 = clean, professionally copy-edited prose with no irregularity; 5 = two or three noticeable slips; 10 = irregularities in most sentences. Count irregularities only. You must NOT judge whether the writing is persuasive, clear or good, must NOT infer carelessness, and must NOT let the prose colour any impression of the underlying science.
proposals.rationale: Rows carrying visible unedited-English slips are consistently dense-high / card-low here: R55 (dense_pct=0.618 vs card_pct=0.179; 'The most GCNs suffer the performance loss when the depth of the model increases'), R54 (dense_pct=0.618 vs card_pct=0.239; 'we task humans with revise each document'), R51 (dense_pct=0.699 vs card_pct=0.303; 'exhibiting potentials to stride towards efficient NAS'). Whether a draft passed through a fluent editor is an upstream fact about the authors' resources and language background whose only visible trace is these slips. Tagged mixed, honestly: the same senior-lab editing pass that fixes articles often also sharpens the experiments.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' first language and their access to a professional copy-edit or a senior in-lab editing pass before submission

proposals.name: Submission-pipeline residue in the text
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which artifacts of the submission or export pipeline survive inside the abstract text: leftover form-field labels and their contents ('Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors...', 'One-sentence Summary: ...'), HTML entities appearing raw ('<='), unrendered markup macros (gammav, Ebb, yv appearing as literal tokens), stray backticks or asymmetric quote marks, conference-edition strings embedded in a URL path. 0 = clean prose with none of these; 5 = one such artifact; 10 = several, or a whole template field reproduced verbatim. Score presence and volume of pipeline residue only. These artifacts carry no information about the research: do NOT read them as sloppiness, and do NOT read their absence as care.
proposals.rationale: R07 reproduces two entire submission-form fields verbatim ('Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors of this work have read and commit to adhering to the ICLR Code of Ethics' and 'One-sentence Summary: ...') and sits at card_pct=0.919 against dense_pct=0.605 -- the residue is extra scoreable matter that a criterion bank can read as a summary statement and an ethics statement. R26 (card_pct=0.393 vs dense_pct=0.056) shows raw unrendered macros where symbols should be, and R25 (card_pct=0.701 vs dense_pct=0.252) shows '<=' entities. Whether a macro rendered or a form field was stripped is a property of the export toolchain and the scraper, upstream of nothing the authors thought about.

proposals.name: Late-entrant corrective framing and crowded-thread markers
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract reads as arriving LATE into an already-worked conversation rather than opening one. Late-entrant fingerprints: titles or framings of the form 'Revisiting', 'Rethinking', 'On the Pitfalls of', 'and Beyond', 'A Unified Perspective on', 'Is X optimal?'; an opening that recites two or more named prior methods before the paper's own move; positioning as a correction, unification, fair re-evaluation, diagnosis, or 'what everyone missed'. Crowded-container fingerprints: 'more and more evidence has shown', 'a growing number of', 'an emerging technique', 'a host of recent work', 'recently proposed', 'several methods extend'. 0 = the abstract opens a topic and names no predecessor; 5 = it names predecessors but proposes a fresh direction; 10 = the entire framing is second- or third-wave commentary on a thread that is explicitly described as crowded. Score how late in the conversation the text positions itself; you cannot see the real submission order. Do NOT judge whether corrective or unifying work is more or less valuable than first-mover work.
proposals.rationale: Late-positioned entries cluster on the scorecard-high side of the disagreement: R33 ('On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond', card_pct=0.752 vs dense_pct=0.466), R03 ('Revisiting Locally Supervised Learning', card_pct=0.692 vs dense_pct=0.402), R13 ('On the Pitfalls of Heteroscedastic Uncertainty Estimation', card_pct=0.675 vs dense_pct=0.154), R52 ('A Unified Algebraic Perspective', card_pct=0.645 vs dense_pct=0.218). The cleanest evidence is the pair inside the slice: R05 introduces fBNNs as a first move (dense_pct=0.427, card_pct=0.107) while R41 arrives afterwards explicitly saying fBNNs 'address this only partially' (dense_pct=0.128, card_pct=0.415) -- the same lineage scores in opposite directions depending on where in the wave the entry sits. A late entrant inherits a fully articulated problem statement and a ready-made list of predecessors to contrast against, which ticks 'motivates the problem' and 'situates in prior work' regardless of what it delivers. Mixed because standing later in a thread genuinely does let an author see further.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item's position in the stream of entries on its topic -- how many entries preceded it and how crowded the subfield already was when it was written and submitted

proposals.name: Formal precision of claims vs vague superlatives
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's central claims are stated with explicit, checkable precision: exact complexity bounds, exact percentages/rates tied to a specific named comparison, or named citations to the specific prior results being beaten. Score 0 if the abstract relies on unquantified adjectives ('remarkable', 'significant', 'considerable', 'state-of-the-art') with no attached number or named comparator anywhere in the text.
proposals.rationale: R24 gives an explicit O(m + poly(k eps^-1)) bound with named comparisons to Feldman&Schulman SODA'12 and Huang et al. FOCS'18, and R51 gives an exact '4.38% of samples' figure -- both dense_high_card_low. By contrast R06 only claims 'remarkable performance gain' with no number, a dense_low_card_high row; precision like this seems to be exactly what a text-only dense reader rewards but a checkbox scorecard does not specifically credit.

proposals.name: One sharp claim vs itemized contribution list
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract is organized around a single, sharp, restatable claim or question that a reader could repeat in one sentence. Score 0 if the abstract is structured as an enumerated list of two or more separate contributions/challenges (e.g. 'first...second...', 'three-fold', numbered '(1)/(2)') such that no single throughline claim dominates.
proposals.rationale: R39 ('Fix your classifier') and R46 (2-simplicial Transformer) each carry one crisp claim and are dense_high_card_low, whereas R47 explicitly frames its contribution as 'three-fold' and R19 is structured around two numbered challenges plus two named model variants (ctx-DocNADE/ctx-DocNADEe) -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Named failure mechanism together with a targeted fix
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific, concrete mechanism by which prior methods fail (a named behavior, bias, or miscounted quantity) AND ties its proposed method directly to correcting that exact mechanism. Score 0 if prior-work criticism is generic ('existing methods are suboptimal/limited') with no specific mechanism named, or if a mechanism is named but the fix is not visibly connected to it.
proposals.rationale: R32 names LOLA's 'arrogant' behavior 'directly at odds with convergence' and proposes SOS specifically to fix that; R54 (MEMO) names the mechanism precisely -- stored models were 'not counted into the memory budget' -- and fixes exactly that accounting. Both are dense_high_card_low. Contrast dense_low_card_high R01 ('none can offer a universal advantage') and R31 ('a laborious task') which never name a mechanism.

proposals.name: Generality claim paired with explicit non-requirements
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly states what the method does NOT require (no retraining, no query access, no labeled data, works off-the-shelf on existing models) as evidence of generality. Score 0 if the abstract never addresses what is dispensable or under what constraints the method still applies.
proposals.rationale: R42 states its attacks 'do not assume any knowledge about or access to the target classifiers' and R40 states SAP applies 'to pretrained networks...without fine-tuning' -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast dense_low_card_high R47, which requires a bespoke hypernetwork and multi-task training procedure with no minimal-assumption framing, and R07, which adds heap-allocation-inspired machinery without ever saying what becomes unnecessary.

proposals.name: Genuine reframing lens vs component-combination language
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reframes a known problem through a genuinely new theoretical/mathematical lens (e.g. causal, information-theoretic, game-theoretic, integral-transform) that unifies rather than concatenates. Score 0 if the core move is described with combination language ('we combine X and Y', 'amalgamate a pool of', 'X together with Y operators') where the contribution is essentially joining two named existing techniques.
proposals.rationale: R30 (FastGCN) reframes graph convolutions as 'integral transforms of embedding functions under probability measures' and R10 (InfoGraph) reframes graph representation learning as mutual-information maximization -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R01 ('GPO uses imitation learning for policy crossover...and applies policy gradient methods for mutation') and R04 ('Optimizer Amalgamation... combine a pool of teacher optimizers'), both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Jargon-to-payoff ratio (new coinages proportionate to insight)
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if any new terms/acronyms the abstract introduces are minimal in number and each is clearly load-bearing for the core idea. Score 0 if the abstract stacks multiple new coinages, acronyms, or borrowed-domain analogies (e.g. a method name plus sub-variant names plus an analogy from an unrelated field) whose relation to the central contribution is not made simple.
proposals.rationale: R07 (Kanerva++) stacks 'locally block allocated latent memory', a heap-allocation analogy, and 'read key distribution'; R19 stacks ctx-DocNADE, ctx-DocNADEe, TM, LM acronyms -- both dense_low_card_high. Contrast R39 and R46, plainly worded with no new coinage, both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Abstract hygiene: freedom from template boilerplate and padding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract is pure scientific content start to finish. Score 0 if the abstract contains leftover submission-template text (e.g. ethics-statement boilerplate, 'One-sentence Summary:' labels) or heavy itemized restatement scaffolding ('First,...Next,...Finally,...') that reads as padding rather than content.
proposals.rationale: R37 literally includes 'Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors of this work have read and commit to adhering to the ICLR Code of Ethics' plus a 'One-sentence Summary:' label pasted into the abstract body; R47 is heavily scaffolded with 'First,...Next,...Finally,...' restatement. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting a component-scoring rubric doesn't penalize this clutter the way a holistic reader does.

proposals.name: Mechanistic account of why the method works, not just that it works
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract gives an analytical, causal, or theoretical account connecting the intervention to the observed outcome. Score 0 if the abstract only reports empirical gains ('outperforms', 'improves by X%') without explaining the underlying reason the method should work.
proposals.rationale: R55 gives a mathematical account linking next-word-prediction pretraining to an O(sqrt(eps)) bound on downstream classification error, and R22 uses influence functions and Hessian spectra to explain why double descent occurs -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R06 ('brings remarkable performance gain' with no explanation of why lane-level reasoning helps) and R34 ('outperforms the state-of-the-art' without explaining why hyperbolic uncertainty specifically drives pacing), both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: One decisive result vs scattered multi-benchmark deltas
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract centers on one (or a small number of) decisive, targeted test(s) of the central claim. Score 0 if the abstract lists many small percentage/parameter deltas across many datasets/tasks with no single result standing out as decisive -- a 'kitchen sink' of incremental wins.
proposals.rationale: R51 centers on one decisive, exactly-quantified result (first exact adversarial accuracy at a specific epsilon on MNIST) and R39 tests one claim broadly ('little or no loss of accuracy for most tasks') -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R49, which lists +1.6% top-1, +0.16M params, +0.07B FLOPs, then separately '3-4% box AP and mask AP', and R19, which lists '6 long-text and 8 short-text datasets from diverse domains' -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Novelty of the question/problem framing itself
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract stakes out a genuinely new question or task definition that did not clearly exist before this framing. Score 0 if the abstract answers a well-worn, already-standard question with an incremental technique.
proposals.rationale: R02 clarifies what 'spurious' even coherently means via a causal common-cause framing, and R38 is explicit that curvature's 'generalization to the emerging domain of hypergraphs has remained largely unexplored' -- both dense_high_card_low, staking new conceptual ground. Contrast R31 (which technique to use for structured linear maps is an old question) and R18 (efficient downsampling for segmentation is a well-worn question), both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Decisive, unhedged claim paired with breadth of claimed regime
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states its result as holding decisively and broadly, without hedging to a narrow regime. Score 0 if the claim is explicitly regime-conditional or hedged ('depends heavily on...', framed as a narrow counterexample or 'one cause among several').
proposals.rationale: R40 frames a decisive minimax solution generalizing 'to pretrained networks, including adversarially trained models' and R42 claims perturbations 'consistently' hurt performance and 'even transfer to unsupervised embeddings' -- both dense_high_card_low, broad and unhedged. Contrast R17, which explicitly says the answer 'depends heavily on what functions we are optimizing,' and R28, whose finding is framed cautiously as 'one cause' via a narrow synthetic counterexample -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Explicit real-world stakes vs purely synthetic/benchmark framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly names a concrete real-world deployment context in which failure would matter (e.g. named high-stakes application domains). Score 0 if the motivation is purely internal to the benchmark/technique with no named real-world consequence.
proposals.rationale: R44 names 'industrial production lines, autonomous vehicles, or healthcare applications' and R52 states 'deploying new policies is costly in real-life RL applications' -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R12 (texture synthesis, purely visual-quality framing) and R45 (SDE learning, purely computational framing), both dense_low_card_high, with no application stakes named.

proposals.name: Named prior-method engagement together with precise improvement claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific prior method or result by name/attribution AND states precisely how the new work improves on or diverges from it. Score 0 if prior work is referenced only generically ('recent work', 'existing methods') with no specific named target.
proposals.rationale: R30 explicitly engages 'GCN...recently proposed by Kipf and Welling' with a precise limitation described, and R32 explicitly engages 'LOLA' with a precise behavioral critique -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R45 ('a host of recent work') and R60 ('these sequence-based models'), both generic and both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Title concision and memorability vs long compound technical title
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the title is short (roughly under 8 words) and evocative/memorable on its own. Score 0 if the title is a long compound-noun technical string (roughly 12+ words) stacking multiple qualifiers.
proposals.rationale: R39's title is 'Fix your classifier' (four words) and R15 uses the catchy 'You Only Need Adversarial Supervision for Semantic Image Synthesis' framing -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R07's 'Kanerva++: Extending the Kanerva Machine With Differentiable, Locally Block Allocated Latent Memory' and R19's 'Texttovec: Deep Contextualized Neural autoregressive Topic Models of Language with Distributed Compositional Prior' -- both long compound titles and both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Claims a previously infeasible capability vs incremental benchmark bump
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract claims to make feasible something previously infeasible or unexplored (explicit 'for the first time', 'has remained unexplored', a new capability class). Score 0 if the claim is an incremental accuracy/efficiency improvement on an already-standard, saturated benchmark with no claim of newly-enabled capability.
proposals.rationale: R38 states hypergraph curvature 'has remained largely unexplored' and R51 achieves an exact adversarial-accuracy certificate 'for the first time' -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R31, which reports an ImageNet accuracy bump 'by up to 5%' on an already-saturated benchmark, and R18, an incremental efficiency-accuracy tradeoff on standard segmentation benchmarks -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Numeric performance-claim density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much of the abstract's text is devoted to specific quantitative performance figures (percentages, point gains, parameter/FLOP counts, benchmark scores). 0 = no specific numbers cited; 10 = the abstract is saturated with concrete numeric claims. Do not judge whether the reported numbers are impressive or whether the work is good; score only the density of numeric-claim language.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('10.9% and 12.4% improvement in Mean Absolute Error') and R44 ('1.6% Top-1 accuracy... 0.16M parameters and 0.07B FLOPs... 3-4% box AP') are both dense_low_card_high and pack in concrete numbers, while R05 and R56 (both dense_high_card_low) report essentially no percentage/point figures. Numeric density plausibly feeds scorecard criteria (e.g. 'empirical rigor') independent of the dense model's holistic read, but could also partly track genuinely stronger empirical results, so it is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Superlative/self-congratulatory phrasing density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract uses superlative or emphatic evaluative language about its own contribution (e.g. 'state-of-the-art', 'significantly', 'remarkably', 'novel', 'outperforms', 'superior'), as a density over the text. Do not judge whether the claims are true or whether the paper is actually good; score only how much boastful/emphatic phrasing is present.
proposals.rationale: R42 ('HYSP outperforms the state-of-the-art on PKU-MMD I...') and R53 ('near-optimal... improves... by up to 5%... over 9%... 36% faster') are both dense_low_card_high and lean heavily on emphatic phrasing, while R24 and R56 (both dense_high_card_low) state their contribution plainly with no superlatives. This is purely rhetorical framing, orthogonal to whether the underlying work is actually strong.

proposals.name: Coined-name-plus-colon title branding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the title follows a 'brand name: description' pattern -- opening with an invented acronym or proper-noun method name, followed by a colon and an explanatory phrase. 0 = purely descriptive title with no coined name; 10 = title is essentially a brand name up front, colon, tagline. Do not judge whether the name is clever or the method good; score only the presence of this titling convention.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('InfoGraph: Unsupervised and Semi-supervised...') and R33 ('FastGCN: Fast Learning with Graph Convolutional Networks...') are both dense_high_card_low, but R40 ('NeRN: Learning Neural Representations for Neural Networks') is dense_low_card_high -- the convention appears on both sides of the disagreement, marking it as a candidate shared nuisance channel rather than a quality marker.

proposals.name: Raw un-rendered math/LaTeX notation density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much raw, un-rendered mathematical notation (literal LaTeX-style symbols/macros, subscripted or superscripted expressions, Big-O style terms) appears directly in the text rather than being spelled out in prose. Do not judge the correctness or sophistication of the mathematics; score only the surface density of literal symbol/markup characters.
proposals.rationale: R05 (dense with terms like the tilde-O sample-complexity bound and epsilon-dependent rates) has card_pct=0.004, the single lowest card percentile in the whole 60-row slice, and R25 (dense with epsilon-coreset and R^d notation, explicit O(...) bounds) has card_pct=0.013, the second-lowest -- both dense_high_card_low. Heavy literal-notation abstracts may specifically depress a criterion-by-criterion scorecard judge without depressing the dense model's holistic read, though it could also partly track genuine theoretical depth, hence mixed.

proposals.name: Explicit code/model-release disclosure sentence
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how explicitly the text announces that code, data, or pretrained models will be or are made publicly available (e.g. a sentence naming a repository or stating that code/models are available). 0 = no such statement; 10 = a prominent, explicit release statement. Do not judge whether release is actually good practice or whether the paper is high quality; score only the presence/prominence of the disclosure sentence.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('Code is available at https://github.com/...'), R21 ('we release our code and models at https://github.com/...'), R44 and R49 all carry an explicit release sentence and are all dense_low_card_high, while it is absent from dense_high_card_low items like R05 and R56. A scorecard 'reproducibility' criterion would mechanically reward this sentence regardless of the surrounding science, though labs with a strong open-source habit may also genuinely be more rigorous, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's/lab's practice in the format (open-source engineering culture)

proposals.name: Large-scale multi-dataset/multi-baseline enumeration
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract emphasizes the scale of its empirical evaluation by explicitly enumerating or counting many datasets, baselines, tasks, or search spaces (e.g. citing a specific large number of baselines/datasets, or listing many benchmark names in a row). Do not judge whether this scale is well-used or the results are good; score only the extent of scale-enumeration language.
proposals.rationale: R26 ('a large-scale experimental protocol comprising 12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks') and R14 ('Experiments with Transformer on OPUS-100 and WMT datasets... massively multilingual settings') are both dense_low_card_high and foreground evaluation scale, while terse single-setup items like R56 (dense_high_card_low) enumerate nothing. Larger, better-resourced teams may also genuinely run more thorough evaluations, so this is tagged mixed rather than purely a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author team size / compute-resource access / lab seniority

proposals.name: Canonical/flagship benchmark-name membership
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the evaluation described in the abstract is anchored in widely-recognized flagship benchmark datasets or environments (e.g. CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, MNIST, MuJoCo, Atari) as opposed to bespoke, niche, or unnamed datasets. Do not judge whether the benchmark choice is appropriate or the results good; score only how canonical/mainstream the named evaluation setting is.
proposals.rationale: R40 ('CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet') and R51 ('binarized MNIST... binarized Omniglot... CIFAR10... ImageNet32x32') are both dense_low_card_high and lean on flagship benchmark names, while bespoke setups like R19 (zebrafish swim-bout classification) and R38 (custom synthetic/real hypergraphs) name no flagship benchmark. A judge or scorer being more comfortable and generous with a familiar setting is a pure recognition/halo effect, not evidence of better work.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/reviewer familiarity with the topic (process dynamics on the receiving side)

proposals.name: Versioned/sequel naming signaling an ongoing research program
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the coined method name signals that this is an explicit sequel or extension of a prior named method (e.g. suffixes like '++' or '*', a version number, or explicit language such as 'extends the X Machine'). 0 = a wholly freestanding name; 10 = an unmistakable sequel/versioning marker. Do not judge whether the extension is a good one; score only the presence of the sequel-naming convention.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('Kanerva++: Extending the Kanerva Machine With Differentiable... Latent Memory') is dense_low_card_high and R07 ('InfoGraph*, an extension of InfoGraph for semi-supervised scenarios') is dense_high_card_low -- the fingerprint appears on both sides of the disagreement, consistent with a shared nuisance channel rather than a quality marker, though an established program could also carry genuine added maturity, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's established research program / seniority / prior practice in the format

proposals.name: Technical acronym/jargon-shorthand density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how many distinct technical acronyms or initialisms (e.g. multi-letter shorthand for methods, tasks, or datasets) are used in the text, regardless of whether they are spelled out on first use. Do not judge whether the acronyms are necessary or well-explained; score only their density.
proposals.rationale: R14 (LS, MNMT, CLSR, OPUS-100, WMT) and R26 (HPO used repeatedly) are both dense_low_card_high and dense with insider shorthand, while R56 and R38 (both dense_high_card_low) spell concepts out with far fewer acronyms. Deep fluency in a subfield's shorthand may also correlate with genuine technical command of that subfield, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's enculturation/fluency in the subfield's insider dialect (practice in the format)

proposals.name: Late-arriving enumerated-contrast positioning
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract explicitly positions itself against multiple enumerated prior alternatives (e.g. naming several competing prior techniques and stating how the current method differs from each, phrases like 'unlike existing methods X and Y' or 'just to name a few'). 0 = presents its idea directly with no such enumerated contrast; 10 = extensive, multi-item contrastive positioning against named priors. Do not judge whether the differentiation is convincing or the work good; score only the extent of enumerated contrastive framing.
proposals.rationale: R49 ('Recent promising techniques draw inspirations from different backgrounds... just to name a few: convex potential layers... Almost-Orthogonal-Layer... This paper introduces a novel algebraic perspective unifying various types...') is dense_low_card_high and R29 ('Unlike quantization-aware training using the straight-through estimator that only targets a specific bit-width and requires access to training data and pipeline, our regularization-based method...') is dense_high_card_low -- both show the late-arriving multi-contrast fingerprint on opposite sides of the disagreement, consistent with it being a position-in-stream nuisance rather than a quality signal, though a later, well-differentiated entry could also be genuinely more mature, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (late-arriving vs early/obvious take)

proposals.name: Mechanistic Fit to Failure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mode and maps each design choice directly to relieving it; score 0 when the method is disconnected from the stated problem or its mechanism is only asserted.
proposals.rationale: R01, R16, and R20 explicitly connect sparse rewards, discrete fluent perturbations, or spatial difficulty to specialized mechanisms, a pattern spanning both disagreement directions.

proposals.name: Proof-to-Procedure Closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal claims directly determine an implementable algorithm, architecture, or parameterization with clearly stated scope; score 0 when theory is ornamental or disconnected from the proposed method.
proposals.rationale: R02, R03, R30, and R48 link convergence, algebraic, complexity, or coreset theory to concrete procedures, especially among dense-high/card-low items.

proposals.name: Boundary-Regime Characterization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract analyzes limiting cases, counterexamples, failure conditions, or regime changes and explains their consequences; score 0 when it discusses only typical operating conditions.
proposals.rationale: R10, R12, R43, and R49 emphasize interpolation thresholds, nonconvergence examples, function-class dependence, or unstable variance estimates, exposing a distinction between the model groups.

proposals.name: Unification with Generative Consequences
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one principled framework recovers multiple existing approaches and yields nontrivial new instances or generalizations; score 0 when the paper merely concatenates or renames existing techniques.
proposals.rationale: R03, R05, R45, and R57 each seek a common mathematical or representational principle that extends beyond a single prior method.

proposals.name: Assumption Transparency and Relief
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when key assumptions are explicit and the method removes an important practical restriction without replacing it with an equally restrictive hidden requirement; score 0 when assumptions are absent, unrealistic, or materially underspecified.
proposals.rationale: R05, R14, and R44 foreground assumptions involving language-model optimality, test distributions, or non-reparameterizable variables, with mixed model treatment.

proposals.name: Quantified Scaling Leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a specific complexity or resource bottleneck, a mechanism that changes its scaling, and a clear usable regime enabled by that change; score 0 when efficiency is only claimed vaguely.
proposals.rationale: R07, R15, R31, and R48 provide explicit complexity, query, verification, or coreset improvements and are concentrated in the dense-high/card-low group.

proposals.name: Mechanism-Isolating Evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation design uses matched comparisons, ablations, stress tests, or controlled variants that distinguish the proposed mechanism from incidental implementation details; score 0 when it reports only aggregate benchmark comparisons.
proposals.rationale: R17, R20, R23, and R35 differ in how directly their evaluations isolate spectral augmentation, adaptive sampling, memory accounting, or ranking-based surrogates.

proposals.name: Cross-Regime Generality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is examined across diverse tasks, domains, architectures, or operating regimes that directly test its claimed scope; score 0 when support comes from one narrow setting.
proposals.rationale: R11, R15, R35, and R45 span many datasets, domains, architectures, or task families, yet receive sharply different model treatment.

proposals.name: Explanatory Diagnostic Yield
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work identifies why a phenomenon occurs, reveals a previously hidden mechanism or artifact, and uses that diagnosis to motivate the method; score 0 when it offers only a technique and performance claim.
proposals.rationale: R05, R10, R37, and R56 provide explanatory accounts of transfer, double descent, experimental artifacts, or likelihood-based OOD failures.

proposals.name: Semantically Grounded Uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract distinguishes the source and meaning of uncertainty and specifies how reliability is assessed under relevant conditions; score 0 when uncertainty is invoked without semantic grounding or reliability analysis.
proposals.rationale: R04, R14, R19, and R49 treat functional, activation, distributional, or heteroscedastic uncertainty in substantially different ways across the disagreement slice.

proposals.name: Native Modeling of Solution Structure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the formulation explicitly represents multiplicity, counterfactual variation, future interaction, or population dependence as part of the task; score 0 when such structured alternatives are collapsed into a single undifferentiated target.
proposals.rationale: R26, R28, R47, and R59 all model alternative labels, valid solutions, future relationships, or population-dependent policies, and mostly belong to the dense-low/card-high group.

proposals.name: Component Necessity and Minimality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every added component has a distinct stated role, an explicit necessity argument, and accounted resource cost; score 0 when a collection of modules is credited only through an undifferentiated total improvement.
proposals.rationale: R13, R18, R22, and R33 present multi-component systems whose individual roles and tradeoffs are central, despite uniformly low dense percentiles.

proposals.name: Architecture-Agnostic Integrability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the core idea plugs into multiple architectures or tasks through a stable, clearly described interface; score 0 when it depends on a bespoke pipeline with no evidence of portability.
proposals.rationale: R06, R18, R29, and R58 describe integration with multiple generators, translation systems, training regimes, or classifier backbones and show opposite disagreement directions.

proposals.name: Algorithmic Reconstructability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when inputs, objective, variables, constraints, and update or inference steps are specified well enough to reconstruct the core method from the abstract; score 0 when the proposal is mainly a name, metaphor, or high-level architectural slogan.
proposals.rationale: R16, R40, R42, and R50 vary sharply in how completely they specify optimization, representation, or architectural details while making broad technical claims.

proposals.name: Claim-Evidence Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are tightly bounded by the described settings, comparisons, and limitations; score 0 when sweeping superiority or generality is asserted from narrow or underspecified support.
proposals.rationale: R18, R33, R53, and R55 use strong broad claims while describing different amounts of scope, tradeoff analysis, and supporting evaluation, making them useful card-high or mixed cases.

proposals.name: Abstract packing and verbosity
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract exhibit dense, extended exposition through long sentences, many clauses, or numerous methodological details? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the feature is good or whether the research is high quality.
proposals.rationale: Length and information packing can affect reading and modeling while reflecting presentation habits rather than research quality. Compare the highly extended exposition in R04 and R46.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission format and authorial space-management practice

proposals.name: Acronym and method-name density
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract introduce or repeatedly use acronyms, branded method names, or named variants? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the names are useful, memorable, or scientifically justified.
proposals.rationale: Naming conventions can make an approach more salient independently of its merit, while practiced naming may also accompany genuinely strong work. Examples include MRLA in R03, InfoGraph and InfoGraph* in R13, and HYSP in R30.

proposals.name: Numeric result specificity
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract contain exact numerical outcomes, percentage gains, point improvements, dataset counts, metric values, or computational speedups? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the numbers are impressive or credible.
proposals.rationale: Specific numbers provide salient evidence-like cues that can influence reception without themselves establishing quality; the reporting practice may also reflect real empirical thoroughness. Examples include R08, R21, and R57.
proposals.upstream_parent: empirical reporting convention and lab writing practice

proposals.name: Formal notation load
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use mathematical notation, Greek symbols, asymptotic expressions, named theorems, or theorem-style claims? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the mathematics is correct, deep, or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Formal notation can signal theoretical sophistication to a reader without being a quality measure, although mathematical training can also contribute to substantive quality. Examples include R38, R50, and R52.

proposals.name: Novelty and superlative rhetoric
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use evaluative or novelty-signaling terms such as novel, first, remarkable, surprisingly, significantly, superior, or state of the art? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether those claims are true or deserved.
proposals.rationale: Rhetorical signaling can shape impressions independently of research quality and may be induced by competitive submission norms. Examples include the language in R03, R28, R47, and R57.

proposals.name: Contribution-template scaffolding
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use manuscript-style scaffolding such as Background/Contributions labels, numbered questions or steps, or explicit First/Second/Finally sequencing? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the organization is good or the contributions matter.
proposals.rationale: Template-like organization can improve skimmability and reader alignment without measuring research quality, though writing practice may also support substantive clarity. Examples include R02, R41, and R45.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format and audience expectations

proposals.name: Artifact and compliance boilerplate
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract contain code links, pretrained-model announcements, ethics acknowledgments, release statements, or one-sentence-summary boilerplate? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the artifacts are useful or the compliance is commendable.
proposals.rationale: Required or customary submission language can create recognizable cues unrelated to scientific quality. Examples include the release and compliance material in R03, R21, R53, and R59.

proposals.name: Canonical benchmark anchoring
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract anchor itself in recognizable benchmark datasets, standard tasks, established architectures, or familiar application names? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the benchmarks are appropriate or the results are strong.
proposals.rationale: Familiar benchmark vocabulary can aid audience recognition and reception without indicating intrinsic quality. Examples include the benchmark lists in R04, R10, R32, and R47.

proposals.name: Late-arrival framing
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract read as a response to a crowded existing line of work by surveying recent methods, listing alternatives, and positioning a gap or refinement? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the gap is real, important, or well addressed.
proposals.rationale: An entry written after obvious approaches have become salient may leave textual traces of crowded-field positioning; that container position is not research quality. Examples include R03, R23, and R55.

proposals.name: Audience-targeted impact framing
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract foreground broad practical stakes, real-world deployment, trust, safety, healthcare, or cross-domain usefulness? Score 0-10 from the text only; do not judge whether the applications are realistic or socially valuable.
proposals.rationale: Application-oriented framing can attract attention from particular audiences independently of research quality. Examples include the deployment and healthcare framing in R02, the trust framing in R32, and the real-world framing in R57.
proposals.upstream_parent: intended audience and social-relevance signaling norms

proposals.name: Bottleneck-to-mechanism fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each stated technical bottleneck maps to a specific design choice; score 0 when the method merely names a problem and stacks components.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R10 explicitly connect coupled constraints to optimization or transition-policy mechanisms, motivating this criterion.

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanatory account
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explains an interpretable causal mechanism linking the method to its intended behavior; score 0 when it offers only architectural description or adjectives.
proposals.rationale: R03 explains which visual features and artifacts drive predictions, while R51 links language-model training mathematically to classification features.

proposals.name: Relevant formal guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theorems or bounds directly concern the central contribution under clearly stated assumptions; score 0 when formal language is decorative or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R20 gives coreset-size and near-optimality claims tied to robust clustering, and R53 connects deployment and sample complexity to explicit lower bounds.

proposals.name: Stress-test coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explicitly addresses realistic adversarial, corrupted, outlier, or failure-case conditions; score 0 when it discusses only nominal operation.
proposals.rationale: R01 centers fluent adversarial perturbations, and R35 addresses exact verification against bounded perturbations.

proposals.name: Resource–quality tradeoff clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when computational, memory, data, or deployment costs are quantified and tied to the proposed mechanism; score 0 when efficiency is asserted without concrete resource accounting.
proposals.rationale: R06 gives complexity reductions, while R13 and R43 make memory constraints central to the method and evaluation design.

proposals.name: Cross-setting generality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one coherent formulation is applied across substantially varied tasks or domains with a shared rationale; score 0 when generality is merely claimed or unsupported by textual scope.
proposals.rationale: R22 spans graph-level and molecular settings, while R40 describes a common encoding-learning approach across architectures, datasets, and tasks.

proposals.name: Contribution isolation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract distinguishes the role of each component through controlled variants or an explicit diagnosis; score 0 when many additions are bundled with no attribution.
proposals.rationale: R14 isolates boundary-focused regularization as protection against degenerate sampling, and R49 identifies the loss formulation as the source of instability.

proposals.name: Evaluation-to-claim alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the described datasets, tasks, baselines, and evaluation dimensions directly match the stated claims; score 0 when broad claims rest on a narrow or mismatched setup.
proposals.rationale: R07 specifies baselines, search spaces, datasets, and tasks matching its HPO claim, while R55 aligns long-term interaction modeling with trajectory datasets.

proposals.name: Assumption and limitation transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract names scope boundaries, conditions, or failure modes under which the method may change; score 0 when it presents the approach as unconditional.
proposals.rationale: R31 distinguishes function classes where random permutations differ, and R49 identifies conditions producing poor heteroscedastic estimates.

proposals.name: Structure-matched inductive bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or architecture encodes a domain symmetry, geometry, or invariant with an explicit reason; score 0 when a generic architecture is applied without structural justification.
proposals.rationale: R06 uses rotational equivariance for spherical data, and R29 derives graph augmentation from spectral structure rather than uniform random perturbation.

proposals.name: Unification with derivation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when prior techniques are unified by a shared formal object and the framework derives meaningful extensions; score 0 when related methods are only listed side by side.
proposals.rationale: R33 generalizes curvature through a common optimal-transport construction, while R52 places several Lipschitz architectures under one algebraic condition.

proposals.name: Problem-reframing precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract defines a neglected problem with explicit objectives and constraints that expose why standard formulations fail; score 0 when motivation remains broad or slogan-like.
proposals.rationale: R18 precisely formulates joint algorithm and metric selection for clustering, and R26 formalizes one-of-many solutions as a distinct structured-output task.

proposals.name: Minimal intervention deployability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method integrates with existing systems using few changes, little retraining, or fixed components; score 0 when deployment requires an elaborate new pipeline.
proposals.rationale: R30 supports post-training bit-width changes, R42 fixes the classifier layer, and R54 applies stochastic pruning without fine-tuning.

proposals.name: Reproducibility specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract names concrete datasets, comparison settings, implementation artifacts, and other protocol anchors; score 0 when it only says that experiments are extensive.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R17 identify datasets and release implementation details, while R36 names multiple datasets and provides code.

proposals.name: Multi-scale dependency modeling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly models interactions across layers, spatial scales, time, or agents and explains their necessity; score 0 when important dependencies are treated independently or locally.
proposals.rationale: R09 targets long-distance relationships in text, R27 uses higher-dimensional attention for relational reasoning, and R55 models future interactions among vehicles.

proposals.name: Acronym-and-brand title packaging
proposals.instruction: How much does the title use a coined acronym, branded method name, slogan-like wording, or memorable title construction? Score only visible presence; do not judge whether it is good or evidence of research quality.
proposals.rationale: A practiced entrant may package methods memorably, which can affect attention independently of merit, while the same practice may coexist with genuine skill. Visible examples include IRIS in R03, HYSP in R20, and MRLA in R52.

proposals.name: Promotional claim density
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use promotional or superlative wording such as “novel,” “first,” “remarkably,” “significant,” “state of the art,” or “outperforms”? Score only wording frequency; do not judge whether the claims are good or true.
