proposals.rationale: Achievement language can influence reader attention without measuring research merit. Such wording is visible in R03, R17, R46, and R58.

proposals.name: Mathematical formalism density
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract contain equations, asymptotic bounds, theorem or proof language, symbolic notation, or named mathematical constructions? Score only formalism extent; do not judge whether the mathematics is good or important.
proposals.rationale: Different research communities routinely expose different amounts of formalism, creating a style signal unrelated to cross-field merit; mathematical fluency may also correlate with genuine quality. Examples include R04, R13, R48, and R58.

proposals.name: Submission-template boilerplate
proposals.instruction: How much does the text contain recognizable template or form-field language, including labeled sections, numbered contribution questions, ethics statements, or one-sentence summaries? Score only boilerplate extent; do not judge whether compliance is good.
proposals.rationale: Template compliance can make text easier to process without describing the underlying research. Explicit traces occur in R23, R51, and R55.

proposals.name: Open-source signaling
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract visibly signal public code, models, datasets, repositories, or reproducibility resources through release promises or URLs? Score only the signaling extent; do not judge whether releasing resources is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Public-release habits can affect discoverability and reader trust independently of research merit, although engineering and reproducibility practice may also accompany genuine quality. Examples include R03, R10, R20, R24, R42, and R52.

proposals.name: Evaluation-breadth signaling
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract enumerate datasets, domains, tasks, baselines, architectures, or experimental settings? Score only the visible breadth of evaluation claims; do not judge whether the breadth is good or sufficient.
proposals.rationale: Access to many datasets, systems, or collaborators leaves a textual breadth signal that can affect perceived scope without itself being research merit; it can also reflect real experimental rigor. Examples include R12, R25, R39, and R53.

proposals.name: Fashionable paradigm vocabulary
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract rely on currently fashionable paradigm labels or trend terms, such as Transformers, self-supervised learning, adversarial robustness, world models, or multilingual scaling? Score only term presence; do not judge whether the topic is good or important.
proposals.rationale: Field fashion changes which labels are familiar and attention-getting, while the labels themselves do not establish research merit. Examples include R03, R20, R54, and R55.

proposals.name: Compressed sentence packing
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract pack many technical claims into long sentences with chained clauses, parenthetical lists, semicolons, or dense enumerations? Score only syntactic and informational packing; do not judge whether the prose is good.
proposals.rationale: Editing and format fluency can alter processing ease independently of research merit, while clearer compression may also reflect genuine communication skill. Visible examples include R12, R28, R43, and R55.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing assistance or author's abstract-writing fluency

proposals.name: Late-riff framing
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract frame its contribution as a revision, alternative, unification, extension, or recombination of several established approaches? Score only this textual framing; do not judge whether the positioning is good, novel, or important.
proposals.rationale: An unseen place in a crowded entry stream could encourage direct, late-arriving recombination language, leaving a trace without measuring merit. Such framing appears in R35, R39, R42, and R49.

proposals.name: Exact-result bookkeeping
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract include precise numerical results, percentages, metric values, parameter counts, FLOP counts, dataset counts, or complexity figures? Score only numerical specificity; do not judge whether the numbers are good or impressive.
proposals.rationale: Mature experimental logging and submission-stage polishing can produce detailed numerical fingerprints that affect concreteness independently of merit, while thorough measurement may also reflect genuine quality. Examples include R21, R24, R47, and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and experimental process maturity

proposals.name: Novel conceptual reframing changing solution approach
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reformulates the problem in a fundamentally new mathematical or conceptual framework that enables types of solutions previously impossible—not merely a new method under the old formulation. Score 0 if the problem is addressed exactly as conventionally formulated using standard approaches.
proposals.rationale: R01 reframes network verification as a mixed integer program, enabling exact presolve-based solutions unavailable to prior methods. R27 reframes OOD detection as statistical hypothesis testing, yielding p-values and Type I error guarantees that heuristic detectors cannot provide. R40 reframes graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures, which directly motivates the Monte Carlo solution. The scorecard likely misses this because it checks surface markers while the dense model perceives the depth of the reformulation.

proposals.name: Explicit provable theoretical guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly states and claims to prove specific theoretical guarantees: convergence, optimality, sample-complexity bounds, or error rates with formal mathematical expressions. Score 0 if no theoretical guarantee is mentioned or claimed.
proposals.rationale: R09 states it is 'first to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence in sample complexity at the same time.' R18 proves 'LookAhead converges locally to equilibria and avoids strict saddles in all differentiable games.' R44 proves its coreset size is 'nearly-optimal.' R57 gives 'theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative.' Dense-low items like R20 and R43 make only empirical claims.

proposals.name: Information density: content per sentence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every sentence introduces a new concept, result, or methodological step with zero filler, generic background, or redundant phrasing. Score 0 if the majority of sentences restate known background, repeat motivation, or contain padding without advancing the contribution.
proposals.rationale: R06 packs an entirely novel architecture, a mathematical generalization of attention, and an application domain into three sentences with no waste. R01 efficiently covers motivation, MIP formulation, presolve algorithm, exact numerical milestone, and comparative results in a compact sequence. Dense-low items like R04 and R41 sprawl across component descriptions and background that dilute the core idea.

proposals.name: Principled mathematical derivation traceable from assumptions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method is explicitly derived from mathematical foundations with the key logical steps visible: assumptions lead to a formulation which leads to the solution. Score 0 if the method is presented as an engineering choice or heuristic without mathematical derivation.
proposals.rationale: R24 derives the L1-gradient regularization by modeling quantization as an L∞-bounded perturbation and analyzing the first-order loss term. R37 derives the training objective from the theorem that KL divergence between stochastic processes equals the supremum of marginal KL divergences. R52 formally shows that ε-optimal language models yield O(√ε) classification error. Dense-low items like R10 and R32 describe architectures without showing the mathematical derivation path.

proposals.name: Unification that generates new methods or bounds
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the framework provably subsumes multiple prior approaches as special cases AND this unification directly enables new methods, tighter bounds, or better complexity that no individual prior approach achieved. Score 0 if prior approaches are merely surveyed or if the unification produces no new capability.
proposals.rationale: R22 presents a generalized spherical CNN framework that encompasses existing approaches and uses the unification to develop two new strictly equivariant layers with reduced complexity O(CL⁴) and O(CL³ log L). R11 generalizes Ollivier-Ricci curvature to hypergraphs via a framework that proves favorable theoretical properties unavailable in graph-only versions. Dense-low R19 attempts algebraic unification of Lipschitz layers but the dense model rates it lower, likely because the unification is retrospective rather than generative.

proposals.name: Sharp identification of fundamental flaws in established methods
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract identifies a specific, non-obvious, conceptual failure mode in a widely-used method—the flaw must be structural or mathematical, not merely 'slightly worse performance.' Score 0 if no flaws in existing methods are identified or only vague limitations are mentioned.
proposals.rationale: R18 shows that LOLA agents can exhibit 'arrogant' behavior 'directly at odds with convergence,' identifying a structural instability in a celebrated method. R31 reveals that storing models in class-incremental learning 'do[es] not consistently work' once memory budgets are fairly counted, exposing a systemic evaluation flaw. R42 shows current state-of-the-art black-box attacks are 'optimal in a natural sense' yet still improvable, a subtle conceptual gap.

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation connecting method to underlying phenomena
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explains WHY the method works at a level deeper than 'it performed better,' connecting effectiveness to identifiable mathematical, structural, or statistical phenomena. Score 0 if only empirical performance results are presented with no explanation of mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R21 connects double descent to 'the spectrum of the Hessian at the optimum,' explaining the phenomenon through an identifiable mathematical object. R46 explains GCN behavior as 'a trade-off of low-pass and high-pass filter which captures the global and local contexts.' R24 explains quantization robustness through the first-order term in the loss expansion. Dense-low R20 reports that layer attention 'can enrich representation power' without explaining the mechanism.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive result challenging field assumptions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the central finding contradicts what the research community would naturally expect, forcing reconsideration of established beliefs or practices. Score 0 if results confirm expected outcomes or apply known techniques as anticipated.
proposals.rationale: R18 reveals that LOLA—a method designed to improve convergence in differentiable games—can actually prevent convergence, which is deeply counterintuitive given its experimental success. R53 shows that fixing the classifier to a Hadamard matrix causes 'little or no loss of accuracy,' contradicting the universal practice of learning the final classification layer. R49 shows classifiers 'fail on their counterfactually-revised counterparts,' revealing that apparently good performance masks reliance on spurious features.

proposals.name: Single dominant insight vs. multi-component aggregation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entire contribution is organized around one clear, sharp idea whose significance is immediately graspable and can be stated in a single sentence. Score 0 if the contribution is a combination of multiple known techniques or sub-modules without a unifying insight that makes the whole greater than the parts.
proposals.rationale: R06 is organized entirely around one idea: higher-dimensional attention via tensor products of value vectors. R14 centers on one framework: hybrid sequence-graph models for summarization. In contrast, dense-low R04 combines population-size encoding, hypernetworks, and multi-task training without a single insight that unifies them. Dense-low R15 combines hyperbolic networks, self-paced learning, and self-supervision as a multi-component system.

proposals.name: Theoretical quantitative precision of claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if claims are stated as exact mathematical bounds, convergence rates, or complexity expressions (e.g., specific Big-O notation with all variables defined). Score 0 if claims use only qualitative language like 'significant improvement' or 'substantial gains' without precise mathematical specification.
proposals.rationale: R09 specifies 'at most ~O(d²H⁵/ε²) trajectories within H deployments,' giving an exact sample-complexity bound. R22 specifies the new layer complexities as 'O(CL⁴) and O(CL³ log L),' and R44 gives the coreset size as 'O(m + poly(k ε⁻¹)).' Dense-low R05 cites percentage improvements (10.9%, 12.4%) without theoretical bounds, and R20 cites accuracy gains without complexity analysis.

proposals.name: Non-trivial cross-domain theoretical bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the work connects two or more distinct theoretical or mathematical areas in a way that imports useful analytical tools or concepts, creating capabilities unavailable within either area alone. Score 0 if the work operates entirely within a single established theoretical framework.
proposals.rationale: R11 bridges differential geometry (curvature), probability theory (random walks), and optimal transport (Wasserstein distances) to define a meaningful curvature for hypergraphs—no single area could produce this. R25 imports game-theoretic mixed strategies from economics into adversarial defense, yielding the stochastic pruning principle. R49 imports the language of causality (confounding, direct effects) into NLP spurious-pattern analysis, providing clarity that standard statistical frameworks lack.

proposals.name: Analysis depth exceeding the proposed method
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the theoretical analysis reveals insights about the underlying problem, phenomenon, or data structure that extend beyond merely justifying the proposed method—i.e., the analysis would be valuable even to someone who never uses the method. Score 0 if analysis is confined to verifying the proposed method's correctness or performance.
proposals.rationale: R21 investigates 'how the loss function affects double descent' and uncovers properties of 'Hessian spectra near the interpolation threshold'—insights about the phenomenon itself, not just a method addressing it. R57 analyzes the 'over-squashing phenomena' in deep graph networks generally, identifying why long-range dependencies fail. Dense-low items like R20 and R54 confine their analysis to their own method's performance metrics.

proposals.name: First-of-kind milestone with concrete evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract claims and demonstrates a specific capability or result never achieved before, with concrete quantified evidence of the milestone (exact numbers, specific problem instances solved). Score 0 if the work is an incremental improvement over prior capabilities.
proposals.rationale: R01 states it determines 'for the first time the exact adversarial accuracy of an MNIST classifier to perturbations with bounded l∞ norm ε=0.1,' with the precise finding of '4.38% of samples' having adversarial examples. R28 shows attacks that make graph neural networks 'perform worse than a simple baseline that ignores all relational information'—a degradation level not previously demonstrated. Dense-low R20 reports incremental accuracy gains on standard benchmarks.

proposals.name: Intellectual value independent of benchmark numbers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper's core intellectual contribution would remain valuable even if all benchmark numbers were removed—the idea changes understanding, opens new directions, or provides a tool others can build on. Score 0 if the paper's entire value is tied to specific numerical improvements on specific benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R06 would remain valuable with no experiments: the 2-simplicial Transformer with tensor-product attention is a new mathematical object. R52's formal proof connecting ε-optimal language models to O(√ε) classification error is valuable regardless of empirical performance. In contrast, dense-low R20's value is entirely its 1.6% accuracy improvement, and R43's value is its mean normalized score of 1.046—remove the numbers and little intellectual content remains.

proposals.name: Articulation of significance beyond the specific task
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract clearly conveys why the contribution matters beyond the immediate task—connecting to fundamental open questions, reshaping evaluation practices, or resolving debates that affect the broader field. Score 0 if the abstract focuses narrowly on task-specific performance without articulating broader implications.
proposals.rationale: R52 frames its work as 'initiat[ing] a mathematical study' of why language models help—positioning the contribution as opening a research direction, not just solving a task. R31 argues that prior CIL comparisons are unfair and reshapes how the field should evaluate memory-constrained methods—a procedural contribution affecting all future work. Dense-low R35 focuses narrowly on zebrafish classification without broader significance, and R55's significance is confined to MuJoCo benchmark performance.

proposals.name: Dense inline mathematical notation
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract contains inline mathematical symbols, Greek letters, or equations. 0 means no mathematical notation, 10 means the text is heavily saturated with equations and symbols. Do not judge the quality or correctness of the math, only the extent of its presence.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts with heavy math notation might intimidate a scorecard or signal deep theory to a dense model. R08 and R55 contain dense inline math (e.g., $mathbb{R}^d$, $epsilon$), which affects text-processing perception but is not a direct indicator of overall research quality.

proposals.name: Reactive trend-riding framing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract reads as a direct reaction to a very recent, highly popular trend by explicitly referencing recent successes or groundbreaking results (e.g., starting with 'Motivated by the success of...'). 0 means entirely independent framing, 10 means explicitly framed as a reaction to a recent popular trend. Do not judge the paper's novelty or quality, only the textual presence of reactive framing.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts like R03 ('Motivated by the success of Transformers...') and R11 ('A recent line of ground-breaking results...') read like late-arriving riffs responding to an existing hype cycle, a textual fingerprint of their position in the research entry stream.

proposals.name: Explicit template boilerplate artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract includes explicit boilerplate artifacts from a conference submission template, such as 'Code of Ethics' acknowledgments, 'One-sentence summary' headers, or explicit URLs to GitHub repositories. 0 means no such artifacts, 10 means multiple explicit template artifacts are present. Do not judge if these are good or bad, only measure their presence.
proposals.rationale: The inclusion of exact conference template phrases like 'One-sentence Summary:' and 'Code Of Ethics:' in R25, or explicit Github links in R14, are artifacts of when and how the submission was compiled, entirely separate from the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Standardized problem-premise phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses standard, boilerplate opening phrases to describe the background problem (e.g., starting with a generic statement about neural networks being successful but flawed). 0 means highly original or specific framing, 10 means extremely generic boilerplate phrasing. Do not judge the quality of the writing, only how standard the problem framing is.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts often begin with rehearsed, generic problem statements. R03 ('Deep reinforcement learning agents are notoriously sample inefficient...') and R39 ('Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached superior performance...') use highly standardized openings that signal an author's practice with the format rather than the quality of their specific contribution.

proposals.name: Large-scale benchmark name-dropping
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract explicitly lists multiple well-known, large-scale datasets or benchmark suites by name (e.g., ImageNet, CIFAR-10, MuJoCo, Atari). 0 means no named datasets, 10 means a long list of named datasets. Do not judge the quality of the evaluation, only count the presence of benchmark names.
proposals.rationale: Naming many large benchmarks is a fingerprint of having the institutional resources to run massive evaluations. Abstracts like R28 (mentioning 86 datasets/tasks) and R37 list numerous benchmarks, which may impress models without necessarily reflecting the conceptual quality of the research.

proposals.name: Catchy acronyms or puns
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the title uses a catchy phrase, pun, or forced acronym (e.g., words formatted as capital letter abbreviations that spell a real word). 0 means a purely descriptive title with no wordplay, 10 means extreme reliance on a pun or acronym. Do not judge whether the title is good or clever, only the extent of wordplay present.
proposals.rationale: Titles in abstracts like R23 ('VariBAD: A Very Good Method...') and R26 ('Fix your classifier...') rely on acronyms and idioms. This is a marketing practice to grab attention and is purely a surface feature unrelated to the actual research quality.

proposals.name: Absence of hedging language
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text uses confident, absolute language without any hedging words (e.g., 'might', 'could', 'we attempt', 'we hypothesize'). 0 means full of hedging and caveats, 10 means completely absolute, unqualified assertions. Do not judge if the confidence is justified, only the extent of absolute phrasing.
proposals.rationale: Highly polished abstracts often remove all uncertainty to sound authoritative, a fingerprint of senior authorship or heavy copy editing. R48 and R35 use entirely declarative, unqualified assertions without any hedging, which may be perceived as higher quality regardless of actual technical merits.

proposals.name: Enumerated structural markers
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses explicit structural markers within the text itself (e.g., 'First,', 'Second,', '1)', '2)', or bolded headers like 'Background:'). 0 means continuous prose, 10 means heavily partitioned by enumerated lists or headers. Do not judge if the markers improve readability, only measure their presence.
proposals.rationale: The use of explicit enumerations like 'First,' and 'Second,' (R09) or explicit lists '1)... and 2)...' (R25) are formatting choices imported from other disciplines or presentation styles. They structure the text but do not inherently represent better machine learning research.

proposals.name: Exotic domain-specific jargon
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract uses highly specialized jargon from a non-machine-learning domain (e.g., specific biology, physics, or medical terms). 0 means pure ML terminology, 10 means heavily saturated with non-ML domain jargon. Do not judge the importance of the domain, only the density of its jargon.
proposals.rationale: Authors crossing over from other fields bring their native jargon, such as the biological terms in R39 ('zebrafish', 'swim bouts') or acoustic terms in R13 ('rectifier wavelet covariance'). This fingerprint of the author's home discipline may distract text models without correlating to the ML quality.

proposals.name: Lengthy multi-claused sentences
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract relies on very long, complex sentences containing multiple clauses, semicolons, or commas. 0 means only very short, simple sentences, 10 means nearly all sentences are extensive and multi-claused. Do not judge the quality of the sentences, only their structural length and complexity.
proposals.rationale: Sentence complexity is a pure surface pattern that might be interpreted as profound by one model or convoluted by another. Abstracts like R08 and R20 feature highly nested, multi-clause sentences that increase text density without necessarily improving the actual research.

proposals.name: Theoretical Guarantees with Clear Assumptions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract provides explicit mathematical proofs, theorems, or formal guarantees (e.g., convergence, strict bounds, non-dissipation) with clearly stated assumptions. Score 0 if the claims are purely empirical, algorithmic, or heuristic without any formal theoretical backing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values rigorous theoretical contributions. DHL abstracts like R03 and R04 explicitly provide theoretical proofs of stability and convergence, which a scorecard model likely misses by focusing on surface-level empirical or algorithmic descriptions.

proposals.name: Identification of Fundamental Conceptual Flaws
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly identifies a conceptual, mathematical, or methodological flaw in well-established prior work and proposes a principled solution to fix it. Score 0 if it only mentions suboptimal performance or proposes an incremental improvement without identifying a fundamental flaw.
proposals.rationale: Pointing out and resolving fundamental flaws, such as unfair memory budgets in R46 or exponential dependence in R38, demonstrates a deep understanding of the field. The dense model perceives this as a marker of high research quality that a rigid scorecard may overlook.

proposals.name: Formalization via Fundamental Mathematical Constructs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is explicitly grounded in mapping the ML problem to a fundamental mathematical domain (e.g., optimal transport, geometry, statistical testing). Score 0 if the method relies on standard ML building blocks (like CNNs or Transformers) without formal mathematical grounding.
proposals.rationale: DHL abstracts frequently leverage deep mathematics, such as Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality in R40 or framing OOD detection as statistical hypothesis testing in R41. This elevates the research quality beyond standard empirical tuning, a distinction the dense model captures.

proposals.name: Unified Generalization of Prior Disparate Approaches
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a single, principled framework that mathematically subsumes or generalizes multiple previously distinct approaches into one cohesive theory. Score 0 if it proposes a narrow method for a highly specific setting without unifying prior work.
proposals.rationale: Generalizing prior work requires a high level of abstraction and insight. DHL abstracts like R23 (unifying black-box attacks) and R53 (generalized spherical CNNs) demonstrate this unifying quality, which is highly valued by experts but may be missed by a checklist-based scorecard.

proposals.name: Explicit Information-Theoretic or Complexity Bounds
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract derives and explicitly states theoretical limits, such as sample complexity bounds, near-optimal rates, or information-theoretic lower bounds. Score 0 if there is no discussion of theoretical limits or mathematical bounds on performance.
proposals.rationale: Deriving bounds, such as the deployment complexity in R18 or the epsilon-optimal error in R60, provides formal guarantees on the fundamental limits of the problem, a hallmark of exceptional research recognized by the dense model.

proposals.name: Game-Theoretic or Bilevel Optimization Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the problem is explicitly formulated as a game (e.g., minimax), an equilibrium, or a nested (bilevel) optimization problem. Score 0 if it uses standard single-level objective optimization (e.g., standard supervised learning).
proposals.rationale: Framing problems as games or bilevel optimizations captures complex, multi-agent, or nested interactions. DHL abstracts like R37 (meta-learning for bilevel attacks) and R56 (mixed strategy games for defense) reflect a sophisticated problem formulation that explains the dense model's high scores.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Explanation of Model Behavior
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explains *why* a method works by analyzing its internal mechanics (e.g., Hessian spectrum, functional space, spectral analysis). Score 0 if the model is treated as a black box and only input-output performance is reported.
proposals.rationale: Understanding the mechanism behind phenomena, such as double descent via Hessian spectra in R14 or quantization effects via loss expansion in R17, provides deep scientific insight that the dense model recognizes as high quality.

proposals.name: Theoretical Insight Prioritized Over SOTA
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's primary focus and claimed contribution is introducing a new mathematical perspective or theoretical understanding, explicitly downplaying or treating empirical state-of-the-art (SOTA) results as secondary. Score 0 if it focuses primarily on achieving SOTA on benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: DHL abstracts (e.g., R24, R50) emphasize conceptual breakthroughs and mathematical formalizations over beating benchmarks. This indicates fundamental contributions that a scorecard overly focused on empirical results might undervalue.

proposals.name: Rigorous Definition of the Threat or Evaluation Model
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract rigorously defines the precise mathematical assumptions, constraints, and properties of the evaluation (e.g., bounded norms, exact error types, strict definitions of robustness). Score 0 if it makes vague claims of 'outperforming' or 'robustness' without formal definitions.
proposals.rationale: Defining exact conditions, such as Type I Error guarantees in R41 or exact adversarial accuracy in R15, demonstrates mathematical rigor in evaluation, separating robust theory from heuristic claims.

proposals.name: Algebraic, Geometric, or Topological Interpretability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed method has an explicit, formal interpretation using algebra, geometry, or topology (e.g., curvature, equivariance, tensor products). Score 0 if the method is an opaque neural architecture with no geometric or algebraic motivation.
proposals.rationale: Interpreting models through geometry or topology, such as Ollivier-Ricci curvature in R24 or rotational symmetries in R53, reveals fundamental structural properties. This represents a deep theoretical angle that the dense model perceives.

proposals.name: Orthogonal or Counterintuitive Problem Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reframes a known problem from a completely different, unexpected, or orthogonal perspective (e.g., treating weight pruning as a mixed strategy game, reformulating classification as sentence completion). Score 0 if it attacks the problem using standard, expected approaches within the existing paradigm.
proposals.rationale: Highly creative work often shifts the paradigm entirely. Reframing classification as sentence completion in R60 or fixing the classifier entirely in R44 represents a profound level of insight that distinguishes exceptional research.

proposals.name: Causal or Information-Theoretic Explanations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract uses tools from causality or information theory to formally explain a previously poorly understood empirical phenomenon. Score 0 if it proposes a new architecture solely to boost performance without explaining underlying phenomena.
proposals.rationale: Using spectral perspectives (R06) or causality (R50) to explain *why* models behave certain ways addresses the root causes of ML challenges, an indicator of profound research quality missed by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Transfer of Deep Mathematical Tools
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract successfully adapts a deep mathematical tool from a completely different field (e.g., algebraic topology, optimal transport) to solve an ML problem. Score 0 if it only uses standard ML or basic statistical tools.
proposals.rationale: Importing advanced tools like 2-simplicial topologies from R35 or duality theorems from R40 to solve ML problems yields novel, high-impact solutions. The dense model captures this interdisciplinary innovation, while the scorecard might just see unfamiliar terms.

proposals.name: Mathematical Decomposition of Objective Functions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract mathematically decomposes a complex objective or loss function into tractable, theoretically justified sub-objectives or bounds. Score 0 if it uses standard, un-decomposed loss functions like standard cross-entropy.
proposals.rationale: Breaking down complex objectives, such as decomposing the functional ELBO in R10 or proving credit assignment efficiency in R21, shows theoretical mastery that often leads to highly principled algorithms.

proposals.name: Derivation of Exact Procedural or Probabilistic Certificates
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method produces exact procedural or probabilistic certificates (e.g., exact p-values, strict equivariance, non-dissipative properties) rather than just approximate predictions. Score 0 if it only provides point estimates or heuristic confidence scores.
proposals.rationale: Delivering exact certificates, such as maintaining strict Type I Error in R41 or proving non-dissipation in R03, provides a level of reliability and formal guarantee that sets top-tier theoretical research apart from purely empirical heuristics.

proposals.name: Acronym and Method Branding Density
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract introduces and repeatedly uses a specific, capitalized acronym or branded name for its proposed method (e.g., 'SNAS', 'PWAN'). 0 means no acronym is used; 10 means the method is heavily branded and repeatedly referenced by its acronym. Do not judge whether the acronym is catchy or good.
proposals.rationale: Branding a method with an acronym is a strategic practice that can signal a polished, ready-to-release package to evaluators, biasing scores independently of the core research quality. R14 and R03 both heavily brand and repeat specific acronyms (SNAS, PWAN), a pattern that models might mistakenly read as an indicator of a paper's significance.

proposals.name: Inline Mathematical Notation Density
proposals.instruction: Rate the density of inline mathematical notation (e.g., variables, norms like $\ell_1$, or big-O complexity). 0 means plain English with no math symbols; 10 means the abstract is heavily interrupted by complex mathematical expressions. Do not judge whether the math is correct, rigorous, or good.
proposals.rationale: The presence of heavy mathematical notation often correlates with theoretical ML papers, which might be scored favorably by models assuming mathematical density equates to rigor, regardless of actual quality. R07 and R59 use frequent inline math symbols ($\ell_\infty$, $O(m + \mathrm{poly}(k \epsilon^{-1}))$), which could act as a confounding signal of technical depth.

proposals.name: Open-Source Code Linkage
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text explicitly includes a URL or a direct mention of open-source code availability (e.g., 'Code is available at...'). 0 means no mention; 10 means a prominent, explicit link and invitation to use the code. Do not judge the quality or usefulness of the code.
proposals.rationale: Explicitly providing a code URL is a practice of well-resourced or community-oriented labs that models might key on as a proxy for reproducibility and paper completeness rather than research quality. R06 and R11 both feature explicit GitHub links, acting as an upstream fingerprint of the authors' release practices.

proposals.name: Explicit Quantitative Benchmark Claims
proposals.instruction: Rate how much the abstract relies on explicit quantitative benchmark claims (e.g., 'improvement of X%', 'ROUGE score', 'state-of-the-art'). 0 means purely qualitative claims; 10 means heavy emphasis on specific numerical improvements. Do not judge whether the benchmarks are impressive or valid.
proposals.rationale: Citing specific percentage improvements or benchmark scores is a stylistic choice that can unduly influence models into perceiving high value, even if the metrics are minor or cherry-picked. R04 and R06 both lean heavily on specific numerical gains (41.16 ROUGE score, 10.9% improvement in MAE), which may bias models independently of the underlying scientific contribution.

proposals.name: Explicit Contribution Boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent of explicit structural boilerplate detailing the paper's outline (e.g., 'Our contributions are three-fold', 'First... Second... Third...'). 0 means a fluid narrative; 10 means a highly rigid, explicitly enumerated list of contributions. Do not judge whether the structure aids readability.
proposals.rationale: The use of rigid contribution boilerplate is a formatting habit taught in academic writing courses that models might mistake for structural clarity or sound logic. R43 ('Our contributions are three-fold') and R45 ('Our contribution is two-fold') exhibit this specific upstream practice, which is predictive of formal submission styles but not research quality itself.

proposals.name: Survey or Unifying Perspective Framing
proposals.instruction: Rate how much the text positions itself as a unifying framework, a survey, or a revisit of a broad known problem (e.g., words like 'unified', 'revisiting', 'bridging'). 0 means a novel, standalone problem; 10 means it explicitly frames itself as synthesizing existing fields. Do not judge the value of the synthesis.
proposals.rationale: Positioning a paper as a 'unified perspective' or 'revisiting' a topic is often an upstream fingerprint of senior researchers who have the breadth to survey a field, which can bias evaluators into treating the text as highly authoritative. R11 and R42 frame themselves this way ('Unified Algebraic Perspective', 'On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond'), blending the author's status with the text's actual quality.

proposals.name: Massive Scale and Resource Markers
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract references large-scale computational markers, such as massive datasets (e.g., ImageNet, OPUS-100), huge model sizes, or intense compute requirements. 0 means small-scale or synthetic data; 10 means heavy emphasis on massive scale. Do not judge if the scale is necessary or impressive.
proposals.rationale: Mentioning massive datasets and industry-standard scale often reflects the authors' institutional compute resources rather than the elegance or quality of the idea itself. R22 and R49 emphasize scaling and large benchmarks ('massively multilingual settings', 'Atari 100k', 'Transformer network'), leaving a textual fingerprint of resource availability that models may score favorably.

proposals.name: Trendy Buzzword Stacking
proposals.instruction: Rate how heavily the title and first sentence rely on integrating currently popular ML buzzwords (e.g., 'Transformer', 'Adversarial', 'Meta-Learning', 'Contrastive'). 0 means standard terminology; 10 means the title/opening feels like a deliberate stacking of trendy keywords. Do not judge if the keywords are used correctly.
proposals.rationale: Authors often stack trending keywords to align with the current conference cycle, which can trick models into perceiving the paper as highly relevant regardless of its actual novelty. R49 and R37 stack multiple hot concepts in their titles and openings ('Transformers are Sample-Efficient World Models', 'TextGrad... Gradient-Driven Optimization'), serving as a temporal tell of the submission's era.

proposals.name: Niche Applied Domain Jargon
proposals.instruction: Rate how narrowly focused the abstract is on a highly specific, non-general application domain (e.g., biology, specific medical imaging, autonomous driving). 0 means a general ML task; 10 means the paper is heavily driven by a highly specific applied science domain. Do not judge the importance of the application.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts steeped in niche applied jargon often originate from domain scientists (e.g., biologists) utilizing ML, which might unfairly penalize or elevate scores depending on how the model weights domain complexity versus pure ML contribution. R25 and R60 focus entirely on niche domains (zebrafish swim bouts, texture synthesis covariance), leaving a fingerprint of the authors' upstream background.

proposals.name: Late-Arriving Reactive Correction
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract reads as a targeted correction or attack on a specific, named, well-known existing algorithm (e.g., highlighting its flaws in the opening). 0 means a completely new problem space; 10 means a direct, reactive rebuttal to one specific baseline. Do not judge if the rebuttal is successful or correct.
proposals.rationale: An abstract that directly attacks a famous baseline often reads like a late-arriving riff from someone who has seen the obvious takes and is trying to carve out a niche. This position in the literature stream is a strong predictor of how the text is received. R42 ('On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond') and R26 ('Fix your classifier: the marginal value of...') explicitly name and call out established methods, leaving a textual fingerprint of their reactive position in the container.
